profile.summary: Ankh is a family of protein language models with an encoder and a decoder, in the shape of a T5 model. You give it an amino-acid sequence and the encoder returns a vector per residue that can be used as a feature for another model, for example to predict secondary structure, localisation or solubility. The authors' stated aim was not scale but protein-specific optimisation: they ran over twenty experiments on masking, architecture and pretraining data to get the same or better results with fewer parameters than the larger models of the time. The later Ankh3 models add a second pretraining task, completing a sequence from its first half, so they can also generate the rest of a sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv 2301.06568 abstract; Ankh README opening lines and Usage; Ankh3 Large model card Model Details

summary_quotes.text: As opposed to scaling-up protein language models (PLMs), we seek improving performance via protein-specific optimization.
We present Ankh, the first general-purpose PLM trained on Google's TPU-v4 surpassing the state-of-the-art performance with fewer parameters
Feature extraction using ankh large example:

Ankh3 is a protein language model that is jointly optimized on two objectives:
* Masked language modeling with multiple masking probabilities
* Protein sequence completion.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The published configuration of Ankh Base is a T5 encoder and decoder: 48 encoder layers and 24 decoder layers at model width 768, 12 attention heads, a feed-forward width of 3072, gated GELU activations and a vocabulary of 144 tokens. Word embeddings are not tied between encoder and decoder. For feature extraction the encoder is used on its own. Pretraining corrupts the sequence with sentinel tokens and asks the decoder to name the missing residues. Ankh3 adds a second task: the first half of the sequence goes to the encoder and the decoder generates the second half. Because Ankh3 was trained on both tasks, its inputs carry a prefix, NLU for representation extraction and S2S for sequence completion.

The idea of this task is to intentionally 'corrupt' an input protein sequence by

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository's model table names four loadable checkpoints: Ankh Large, Ankh Base, Ankh3 Large and Ankh3 XL, each with a Hugging Face repository. A result must name which of them it used, and should pin the revision, since the cards are updated in place; the revisions read here are d99cb6b9 for Ankh Base, 74b371db for Ankh Large and 2be09162 for Ankh3 Large. For Ankh3 there is a further choice inside the checkpoint: the card says the NLU prefix is used for the encoder representation and suggests trying the S2S prefix instead, because it can give better embedding quality, and the repository's own result tables report Ankh3 numbers separately for NLU and S2S. The tables also list a model called Ankh 2 Large, which has no loader and no Hugging Face link in the sources read.

sections.title: Downstream heads and licence
sections.body: The ankh package ships more than the language models. It also has small ConvBERT heads for binary classification, multi-class classification and regression, meant to sit on top of the embeddings, and a function that computes a pseudo-likelihood for a sequence. The datasets used in the original evaluation are listed as Hugging Face datasets, including secondary structure sets, DeepLoc, fluorescence and solubility. The licence is the thing to check before using any of this in a product: the pretrained models are released under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0, which the Hugging Face cards also declare, so commercial use is not permitted.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: General-purpose protein language model, encoder and decoder in the T5 shape, used mainly as an encoder for per-residue representations; Ankh3 can also complete a sequence.
facts.source_locator: arXiv 2301.06568 abstract; ankh-base config.json; Ankh3 Large model card

quotes.text: We present Ankh, the first general-purpose PLM trained on Google's TPU-v4

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: T5ForConditionalGeneration. Ankh Base: 48 encoder layers, 24 decoder layers, d_model 768, 12 heads, d_ff 3072, gated GELU, vocabulary 144, untied word embeddings. The configurations of the other checkpoints were not read.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: An amino-acid sequence. For Ankh Base and Large the README's example passes it as a list of single characters with is_split_into_words set to true. For Ankh3 the string is passed whole with a prefix, NLU for embeddings or S2S for completion, and the tokenizer must be T5Tokenizer rather than AutoTokenizer.
facts.source_locator: Ankh README Usage, feature extraction example; Ankh3 Large model card How to use

quotes.text: # Make sure that you must use `T5Tokenizer` not `AutoTokenizer`.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Encoder embeddings, one vector per residue, which the repository's own downstream heads take at input dimension 768 for the base model. Ankh3 can also generate the remainder of a sequence, and the package can compute a pseudo-likelihood for a whole sequence.
facts.source_locator: Ankh README Usage, feature extraction, downstream models and likelihood examples; Ankh3 Large model card For Sequence Completion

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: Not reported as counts. The paper gives only relative figures against the state of the art of the time, fewer than 10 per cent for pretraining, fewer than 7 per cent for inference and under 30 per cent of the embedding dimension, and the Hugging Face API returns no safetensors parameter count for any of the three checkpoints read. The Ankh Base config gives d_model 768 with 48 encoder and 24 decoder layers.
facts.source_locator: arXiv 2301.06568 abstract; Hugging Face API responses, which return no safetensors block; ankh-base config.json

facts.value: Not reported. No maximum sequence length is stated for any Ankh checkpoint in the sources read. The Ankh Base config uses relative position buckets, with relative_attention_num_buckets 64 and relative_attention_max_distance 128, which are attention settings rather than a length limit. The pseudo-likelihood helper has a shard_input option, which implies long sequences are split.

run_guide.summary: Install the ankh package and get per-residue embeddings for two sequences, then the Ankh3 variant of the same task.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and transformers; the sources read pin no versions.
torch must be imported for the README example, which uses torch.no_grad without importing it in the snippet.
The weights download from the Hugging Face hub on first use and are not gated.
The weights are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so non-commercial use only.
No GPU requirement or memory figure is given in the sources read.

steps.title: Install
steps.explanation: The README's installation command. It brings the loaders, the ConvBERT heads and the pseudo-likelihood helper.

steps.title: Get embeddings from Ankh Large
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import ankh

model, tokenizer = ankh.load_ankh_large()
model.eval()

protein_sequences = [
  'MKALCLLLLPVLGLLVSSKTLCSMEEAINERIQEVAGSLIFRAISSIGLECQSVTSRGDLATCPRGFAVTGCTCGSACGSWDVRAETTCHCQCAGMDWTGARCCRVQPLEHHHHHH', 
  'GSHMSLFDFFKNKGSAATATDRLKLILAKERTLNLPYMEEMRKEIIAVIQKYTKSSDIHFKTLDSNQSVETIEVEIILPR',
]

protein_sequences = [list(seq) for seq in protein_sequences]

outputs = tokenizer(
  protein_sequences, 
  add_special_tokens=True, 
  padding=True, 
  is_split_into_words=True, 
  return_tensors="pt",
)
with torch.no_grad():
  embeddings = model(input_ids=outputs['input_ids'], attention_mask=outputs['attention_mask'])
print(embeddings.last_hidden_state.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's feature extraction example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. The import of torch and ankh and the final print were added, because the README snippet assumes them. Replace load_ankh_large with load_ankh_base for the smaller model.

steps.title: Or embed with Ankh3 Large through transformers
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5ForConditionalGeneration, T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch

sequence = "MDTAYPREDTRAPTPSKAGAHTALTLGAPHPPPRDHLIWSVFSTLYLNLCCLGFLALAYSIKARDQKVVGDLEAARRFGSKAKCYNILAAMWTLVPPLLLLGLVVTGALHLARLAKDSAAFFSTKFDDADYD"

ckpt = "ElnaggarLab/ankh3-large"

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained(ckpt)

encoder_model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained(ckpt).eval()

nlu_sequence = "[NLU]" + sequence
encoded_nlu_sequence = tokenizer(nlu_sequence, add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors="pt", is_split_into_words=False)

with torch.no_grad():
  embedding = encoder_model(**encoded_nlu_sequence)
PY
steps.explanation: The Ankh3 Large model card's embedding example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. Note the NLU prefix and that T5Tokenizer must be used, not AutoTokenizer. The card suggests the S2S prefix may give better embeddings for some uses.

notes: Watch the licence on this one. The weights are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which is not among the identifiers the brief allows on a source record, so no source here carries a licence field and store_bytes is false for the README and the model card. The README's licence sentence names Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 but links to the plain by/4.0 deed; the Hugging Face card metadata of all three checkpoints read says cc-by-nc-sa-4.0, so the text, not the link, is what the structured rows follow. The code licence is unknown: the README's licence section covers only the pretrained models and no other source read gives a code licence, so code_licence is null in every structured row. The Ankh3 XL row was written from the README table alone, since its Hugging Face metadata was not fetched, so its gated field is null. The repository's result tables also name Ankh 2 Large, with no loader and no download link, so it is not listed as a checkpoint. The record's existing source is the HyPLM technical report, which was not fetched; this page is written only from Ankh's own documentation.
